passage.title: The Race to Reclaim Battery Metals

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The electric vehicle (EV) transition was built on the premise of cleaner transport, but it has given rise to a new problem: what to do with the batteries once they can no longer power a car. As the first generation of EVs approaches retirement, the industry is finding that a lithium-ion battery is less a disposable component than a concentrated bundle of scarce metals such as nickel, cobalt, lithium, copper and graphite. Managing this material is no longer a marginal environmental concern but a question of resource security. The emerging answer is a circular economy in which spent batteries are treated as 'urban mines', with recycling and reuse seen as strategic priorities for governments and manufacturers alike.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the challenge is considerable. One industry report estimates that retired EV batteries worldwide exceeded 280,000 tonnes in 2026, while the global recycling market was valued at roughly 12.99 billion US dollars in 2025 and is projected to reach 16.44 billion dollars in 2026. In China alone, around 43 GWh of EV batteries are expected to reach the end of their useful life in 2026, rising to 171 GWh by 2030. The wave has been slower to arrive in other regions, partly because many batteries remain in service for eight to twelve years. As a result, manufacturing scrap from gigafactories already supplies much of the current feedstock, while most end-of-life packs are still years away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Three broad technical routes dominate commercial recycling. Pyrometallurgical processing, essentially smelting in a high-temperature furnace, is flexible and robust but weak on lithium, recovering less than 60 percent of that metal while capturing 90 to 98 percent of nickel and cobalt. Hydrometallurgical processing, which involves leaching shredded 'black mass' with chemical solutions, achieves higher overall performance, with nickel and cobalt recovery of 95 to 99 percent and lithium recovery of 85 to 95 percent. A newer route, direct recycling, restores the structure of cathode materials rather than breaking them down. It promises the lowest energy consumption and highest material yield, but requires tightly controlled feedstock and remains at an earlier stage of commercialisation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A handful of companies now operate at commercial scale. Redwood Materials, founded by a former Tesla executive, reported in late 2025 that it had raised 350 million US dollars and was recovering roughly 95 percent of lithium, nickel, cobalt and other materials at its South Carolina facility. Belgium's Umicore runs a 150,000-tonne plant at Hoboken that combines smelting with hydrometallurgical refining. China's CATL Brunp, described as the world's largest recycler, claims combined recovery rates of 99.6 percent for nickel, cobalt and manganese and 96.5 percent for lithium. In August 2025 the mining and trading giant Glencore completed its acquisition of Li-Cycle, folding the Canadian firm's hydrometallurgical technology into its global refining network.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Regulation is now a powerful driver. The European Union's Battery Regulation, in force since 2023, requires that at least 65 percent of a lithium-ion battery be recycled by 2025 and 70 percent by 2030. It also sets material-specific targets: lithium recovery must reach 50 percent by 2027 and 80 percent by 2031, while cobalt and nickel must reach 90 percent and 95 percent respectively on the same timetable. From 2031, new batteries sold in the EU must contain minimum recycled content, including 16 percent for cobalt and 6 percent for lithium. A digital battery passport, mandatory from February 2027, will record material origin and carbon footprint, linking recyclers and manufacturers in a single documented chain.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recycling has also acquired a geopolitical rationale. In its Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, the International Energy Agency warned that China accounts for roughly 72 percent of global refined supply of critical minerals, including virtually all spherical graphite used in battery anodes. The report noted that lithium prices more than doubled between January 2025 and April 2026, while cobalt prices surged by around 130 percent after the Democratic Republic of the Congo imposed export quotas. It projected persistent deficits for lithium, cobalt and graphite through 2035, and estimated that sources outside China would meet only about 10 percent of graphite demand in 2030. In this context, recycled material is increasingly framed as a hedge against supply disruption.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Not every retired battery goes straight to the shredder. A pack that can no longer provide the range a driver expects typically retains 70 to 80 percent of its original capacity, often enough for stationary energy storage. In British Columbia, Moment Energy opened what it calls the world's largest EV battery repurposing facility in June 2026, aiming to produce one gigawatt-hour of storage systems by 2030. In Texas, B2U Storage Solutions operates a ten-megawatt project built from more than 720 repurposed EV batteries, and has agreed to receive packs from Waymo's autonomous vehicle fleet. Such projects store cheap midday solar power and release it when prices rise, extending the useful life of materials before eventual recycling.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Despite the momentum, obstacles remain. Feedstock quality varies widely, since different chemistries require different processing, and a facility designed for one mix can face margin pressure when the supply changes. Pretreatment and logistics are costly, and the economics depend on metal prices that remain volatile. Moreover, recycled-content mandates do not yet exist in every market, leaving some producers to wait for regulation rather than lead it. Nevertheless, with supply security, environmental pressure and regulatory deadlines converging, most analysts expect battery recycling to become a permanent feature of the automotive and energy landscape.
